The estate claims Fairfax County's lack of immigration enforcement violates federal law.Â

FAIRFAX, Va. (CN) âThe family of a murdered Virginia woman sued Fairfax County Friday, claiming the local government’s lax approach to immigration enforcement caused her death.

Cheryl Minter, mother of Stephanie Minter, sued the county board of supervisors and Sheriff Stacey Kincaid, claiming they conspired to prevent authorities from securing equal protection under the law. The lawsuit follows the February fatal stabbing of Minter at a bus stop, which prosecutors have charged Abdul Jalloh, who entered the U.S. illegally from Sierra Leone in 2012, with committing.

Jalloh faces a second-degree murder charge and has a criminal history that includes more than 30 arrests for offenses including rape, malicious wounding and assault. Minterâs estate blames county policies restricting cooperation between local law enforcement and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“Stephanie’s family deserves to know whether county policies stopped local officials from cooperating with ICE after a man with a violent history was set free,” America First Policy Institute Chair of Litigation Chad Mizelle, who is representing the estate, said in a statement. “When law enforcement warns that someone is dangerous, local leaders should back them with every lawful tool available.”

Jalloh served only part of his sentence for a 2023 malicious wounding conviction before returning to the community. Police arrested him again in May 2025 after he reportedly stabbed a sleeping person in the leg. Prosecutors, including Fairfax County Commonwealthâs Attorney Steve Descano, dropped the charges, reportedly citing difficulties getting unhoused people to testify in court.

“There was one option for protecting Fairfax County residents that no member of the Fairfax County justice system was even allowed to explore: having Jalloh detained by federal immigration enforcement authorities,” the estate wrote.

According to the estate, Fairfax County and its sheriffâs office have adopted policies since 2018 that restrict local law enforcement from detaining people subject to administrative immigration requests without judicial warrants or sharing personal information, including release dates, with immigration officials. Fairfax County, a wealthy Washington, D.C., suburb, is the commonwealth’s largest jurisdiction.

The estate argues that local law enforcement repeatedly warned about Jalloh before his final release and that the countyâs policies violate federal law by unlawfully benefiting immigrants without legal status.

“The co-conspirators chose to tie the hands of their staff by preventing them from using the most effective means of protecting Fairfax County residents from Jalloh, and instead prioritized their goal of shielding illegal aliens from federal law,” the estate said.

A Fairfax County spokesperson told Courthouse News that the county hadn’t been served with the lawsuit and that it doesn’t comment on pending litigation. The Fairfax County sheriff’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

“For so many years, Angel Families across the country were abandoned, left to grieve tragedies that should never have happened in the first place. There has been zero accountability and no avenues for justice,” Nicole Kiprilov, president & founder of The American Border Story, said in a statement.

“The American Border Story has stood alongside Cheryl Minter since the brutal murder of her daughter, and we believe AFPI’s lawsuit has the potential to open the door for other Angel Families to seek accountability from jurisdictions whose policies have stolen countless American lives.”

Descano and Kincaid testified before the U.S. House Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security and Enforcement in May at Republican Congressman Jim Jordanâs request, facing questions from Republican lawmakers about the countyâs policies.

In 2025, then-Governor Glenn Youngkin directed then-Attorney General Jason Miyares, both Republicans, to investigate the policies. Miyares identified six instances in which the county reportedly gave lenient treatment to immigrants lacking permanent legal status who were accused of violent crimes, including rape and malicious wounding.

“The death of Stephanie Minter was a direct and proximate result of the co-conspiratorsâ joint efforts to violate federal immigration law,” the estate said.

#7555. Back in lower court, Amazon wants to continue suit against AI assistant

Amazon argues Perplexity's Comet tool is accessing the online shopping giant without authorization.

SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â âI really don’t know what to do with this case,â Senior U.S. District Judge Maxine Chesney said Friday as a legal fight between Amazon and Perplexity AI returned to her court.

By the end of the three-hour hearing, the Bill Clinton appointee had granted Perplexity’s request for a stay in discovery, saying it would keep costs down and give her time to consider a dismissal motion. Neither Amazon nor Perplexity immediately responded to requests for comment.

Perplexity is the developer of Comet, an AI web browser capable of shopping on Amazon, including by comparing prices and reviews.

Amazon argues the tool violates laws like the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Chesney previously found that Amazon would likely succeed on those arguments â then a Ninth Circuit panel rejected her findings, sending the case back to her court.

In its ruling, the Ninth Circuit found Chesney erred in her analysis of rules prohibiting access âwithout authorizationâ or at a level âexceeding authorized access.â

“It is the user who âaccessesâ Amazonâs computers with the help of the assistant,” U.S. Circuit Judge Milan Smith Jr., a George W. Bush appointee, wrote for the panel. A claim by Amazon under the California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act failed under the same logic.

On Friday, Chesney asked Amazon and Perplexity how she should apply the panel’s ruling.

Hagan Scotten, an attorney with the firm Hueston Hennigan who is representing Amazon, told the judge there were new facts that the appeals court had not considered.

A new version of Comet had been released since the panel’s decision, Scotten said. He also said Perplexity employees had tested versions of Comet on Amazon.

Scotten also argued the panel did not fully understand how Comet works.

The judges, he said, mistakenly believed that Comet only shopped on Amazon when directed by a user to do so. In fact, he said, a user might simply ask Comet to buy an item, then the tool would go to Amazon without being “invited in.”

âPerplexity and Perplexity alone is sending the agent to Amazon, which answers the panelâs question about who is in control here,â Scotten said, describing Perplexity as a “rogue actor” that was violating Amazon restrictions on AI tools.

âYou are very persuasive,â Chesney told Scotten. Nonetheless, she said she was trying to be âvery careful [so] you donât take me down another path that results in a reversal.â

Representing Perplexity with the firm Quinn Emanuel, attorney Daniel Posner pushed back on Scotten’s claims, including the argument that facts had changed since the Ninth Circuit ruling.

Comet cannot access Amazon itself, he said. Instead, a user must give the AI assistant access to their Amazon account.

âThe user always directs the agent to do something," he said. “That is the underpinning of the Ninth Circuit ruling.”

Posner argued Amazon was “scraping the barrel” in an effort to save its case. He cited Amazon’s claims that Perplexity employees were accessing Amazon.

âAs I understand, the allegation is that some unspecified number of Perplexity employees used their own Amazon accounts to access Amazon," he said. “If that type of conduct is criminalized, that would hit the panel opinion head-on.”

After adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a new lower-court ruling.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

Also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

On Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

The December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”

On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”

In a column for The New York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

In a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

In a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” said Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”

On Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”

Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

By Jordan J. Ballor & Logan Tantibanchachai

In a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan J. Ballor and Logan Tantibanchachai reflected on Democrats’ recent embrace of court packing, which they “define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.” Such an approach to court reform “risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently,” they wrote.

In his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored what Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could mean for a challenge to an Iowa law criminalizing certain immigration-related conduct, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Because Iowa’s Republican attorney general lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, it’s now unclear if the state will move forward with its defense of the law, “providing yet another reason why elections matter.”

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky revisited the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, during which several conservative justices appeared to suggest “that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.” Such an approach to free exercise would be at odds “with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact ... is not enough to prove discrimination,” Chemerinsky contended.

In her In the Interim column on Monday, Taraleigh Davis revisited comments made by Justice Samuel Alito this fall about the court’s emergency docket, including why it’s so busy these days. The data, according to Davis, “support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the nature of lame-duck confirmations after the showdown between Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, journalists’ records, and weakening the presidential veto.

Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka continue their discussion on the significance of and fallout from this month’s midterm elections.

The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two New Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, New Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

Woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He quickly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

During the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” New Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

In 1823, the New Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

In 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

In 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of New Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

In 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”

In 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of New York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

Woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun said – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

MR. MILLER: “– No, I think they mean what a district judge honoring his Article III commission concludes after an intensive evaluation of the entirety of the complaint, looking for that strong inference, putting on his sort of motion to dismiss 12(b)(6) hat, says okay –”

MR. MILLER: “– No, I did not mean that. Don't take me literally on that. For heavens sakes, I'm from Brooklyn. I'm very colloquial. I'm very sorry about that.”

JUSTICE SCALIA: “Let me write that down. We should not take you literally. All right.”

— Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

JOHANNESBURG (AP) â Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.

Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021.

The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa’s first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country’s first democratically elected leader.

Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa’s struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women’s rights and gender equality.

âPhumzile Mlambo-Ngcukaâs fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl,â he said in a statement Friday.

U.N. Women said her courage inspired people around the world and her leadership helped shape a global movement.

âFrom her early days as an anti-apartheid activist to becoming South Africaâs first woman Deputy President, and later leading U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021, she devoted her life to justice and equality,â the agency said in a statement.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was appointed deputy president during a volatile era in South African politics and for the ruling ANC, which was experiencing infighting and a bruising succession battle. She replaced former Deputy President Jacob Zuma when he was fired after being implicated in a corruption scandal involving an arms deal.

Despite her known history as a political activist and experienced lawmaker, her appointment drew criticism over her marriage to Bulelani Ngcuka, the country’s lead prosecutor who was pursuing corruption charges against Zuma.

She is survived by her husband and their five children.

Two drones attacked the vessel in âneutral watersâ 3 nautical miles (5.6 kilometers) from the Russian border, Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of Russiaâs Leningrad region, wrote on Telegram. He later said the crew had not needed to be evacuated and that the situation on board was âunder control,â with preparations being made for the vessel to resume navigation.

The ship drifted into Finnish territorial waters, the Finnish Border Guard said in a statement, adding that it posed no danger to maritime traffic. Finnish border guards were carrying out a rescue operation and preparing for possible environmental damage, it said.

According to a statement sent to Estonian media, Estonian authorities received a report that a fire had broken out on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was sailing in the Gulf of Finland. The ship had drifted out of Estoniaâs exclusive economic zone earlier Saturday. According to preliminary reports, explosions occurred on board.

âWar is spilling into our immediate vicinity,â Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, between Poland and Lithuania.

Finlandâs Defense Ministry also said that a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace around noon Saturday, flying about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) into the country. Defense Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said the incident may have been related to rescue or monitoring operations involving the damaged ship.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, 11 people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the Kharkiv region, Ukraineâs State Emergency Service said Saturday. One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

#7546. Exam shows that the hat Fiona the hippo ate was deep in her small intestine

A postmortem examination revealed that a swallowed hat became lodged in Fiona the hippoâs digestive tract, leading to her death at the Cincinnati Zoo.

CINCINNATI (AP) â A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.

Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.

The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.

Since her death, Fiona’s fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats. âShe brought so much love in her lifetime,â said one note.

Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many â from teachers to parents to children.

During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for âanyone that was going through hard times.â

Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years.

âThe support that weâre feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. “She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles.â

One of Fiona’s keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member.

âIt has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire,â Wingate wrote. âWe lost her in the most horrific and tragic way.â

She ended: âShe was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry.â

Fiona wasnât the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object.

In 1923, a hippo âcame to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth,â according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippoâs remains from the Cincinnati Zoo.

The Cincinnati Enquirer reported at the time that Zeekoe had a habit of opening his mouth wide to chomp cake and other treats tossed by guests. He died after swallowing a tennis ball, which zoo officials believed a child had dropped into the hippoâs mouth without realizing the harm it could cause.

Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona’s digestive system wasn’t meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said.

Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through.

Blood work showed her health was failing Thursday, so the zooâs animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, said Mike Wenninger, the zooâs director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippoâs anatomy, he added.

Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he said.

The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines.

âNo treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked,â Wenninger said.

Jenike called the zoo’s staff heroic in their efforts to save her.

At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.

But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.

The zoo’s animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.

Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries.

Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.

Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure âthe smiles she gave me.â

Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.

The zoo’s staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn’t nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.

She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.

Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

By OBED LAMY and JOHN SEEWER Associated Press

Associated Press journalists Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

#7544. Voters oust some sheriffs who signed pacts to help Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts

Some sheriffs who cooperated with the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts lost their reelection bids as challengers pushed for changes in local law enforcement.

GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) â As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administrationâs immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County’s growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with âsheriffâ made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

âTheyâve been living in fear. They feel like they donât have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they donât belong,â Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriffâs deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trumpâs push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trumpâs crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration’s efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under whatâs known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate’s defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse â from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff’s office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations â including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement â that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker âNo Chance Alamanceâ because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn’t and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community â and to some extent, the Black community â feared engaging with the sheriff’s office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriffâs cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the countyâs first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson’s record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn’t think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

The sheriffâs office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Since 2008, the county detained and turned over 1,884 people to ICE, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said. But that came to a halt this year when Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

âIn general, people are fed up with the sheriffâs negativeness about immigrants,â said retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, who distributed emails, social media posts and campaign literature in support of Bickel.

In Wisconsinâs Winnebago County, ICEâs arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

âAny kind of perceived alignment definitely is considered a liability at this point,â said Molly Smiltneek, a local advocate and immigration lawyer who attended a vigil for the teacher.

Though the sheriffâs department had nothing to do with the teacherâs arrest, its 287(g) agreement became central to the campaign, boosting Democrat Jason Rippl, who promised to end it.

Long, who formerly worked as a deputy in a neighboring North Carolina county, said he will uphold the law in his new role and hold offenders accountable. But he said he won’t participate in the 287(g) program.

He has set up meetings with the Latino community in the hopes of building new relationships.

âI want them to see the sheriffâs office in the community, creating a partnership, letting them know that they have a voice. â¦ Thereâs no need to operate in fear,â he said.

By SARAH RANKIN, MIKELLA SCHUETTLER and DAVID A. LIEB Associated Press

Schuettler reported from Phoenix and Lieb from Jefferson City, Missouri. Associated Press journalist Allen G. Breed contributed from Graham.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

#7542. Criminal law is constitutional law

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law

Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

“[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

But why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”

There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution

This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.)

Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure

Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

Why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

(Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.)

In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution

In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it says,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law

Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law

By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/

#7536. As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a new batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.

Last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at New York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and showed off projects from creators like Ms. Rachel, Brave Wilderness, Dhar Mann, Deestroying, and Cleo Abram.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.

Google President Sean Downey took the stage to highlight YouTube’s continued dominance on TV screens, and gave a nod to participating creators for fueling the UGC machine that keeps viewers coming back to YouTube–on TVs and across other devices.

Of course, he also appealed to advertisers in the same breath, reminding them that this “world-class” content is what they could be marketing alongside, if they cough up the cash to Google.

“YouTube creators are not just shaping modern culture, they are redefining the entire entertainment landscape. This slate of shows demonstrates how creators are commanding primetime attention on the big screen and building unmatched fan loyalty,” Downey said. “For brands, this isn’t about buying thirty seconds of ad space; it’s about moving past standard commercial breaks and partnering directly with the storytellers who are defining modern culture.”

YouTube has spent years at the top of TV watch time charts–a fact that really gets under the skin of competitor Netflix. Up till recently, though, Netflix’s main response to this irritant was talking a lot of sh*t about YouTube and occasionally signing back catalog deals with view-drivers like Ms. Rachel and CoComelon.

But in the last 12 months, something’s shifted. Netflix has begun tapping creators like Salish Matter, Alan Chikin Chow, and the Stokes Twins not for back catalog agreements, but for development deals–deals which result in exclusive original programming that won’t appear on YouTube.

And YouTube’s not happy about it. The platform has been offering creators money, including production financing and sweet ad deals, in exchange for turning down offers from Netflix. Conversely, creators who decide to sign with Netflix are put on YouTube’s naughty list, and denied perks like revenue shares from primo ad deals.

(That being said, Netflix-friendly creators aren’t entirely blacklisted. DiGiovanni signed a catalog crossposting deal with Netflix in July, and was still one of the headline creators at tonight’s showcase.)

The point we’re making here is this: With Netflix–and Disney–sniffing around, YouTube has more incentive than ever to hype up its creators and their projects on a big stage.

Nick DiGiovanni | Chef | New series live now on a dedicated YouTube channel

Chef Nick DiGiovanni, the creator behind the world’s largest food YouTube channel, launches Chef (@Chef) – a new series from his production company, Knife Drop Studios. After reaching billions of viewers through his global culinary adventures (@NickDiGiovanni) and step-by-step recipes (@NicksKitchen), DiGiovanni is now turning the camera solely toward fellow professional chefs, offering an unfiltered look inside kitchens around the globe. From Michelin-starred restaurants and hidden street food gems showcased in full-length episodes, to POV recipes in short-form episodes, Chef puts viewers in the shoes of the people behind the scenes, offering a unique, captivating perspective for everyone from the culinary obsessed to the simply curious. You can view the first full-length episode, “Inside the World’s #1 Pizza Restaurant” now, only on YouTube, along with the first short-form POV episode, “Butter Chicken Shawarma”. New short-form POV episodes will debut daily across Nick’s newly-launched @Chef channel with full-length episodes rolling out throughout 2026-27 exclusively on YouTube.

Morgan Jay | Music Therapy with Morgan Jay | New series premieres Nov. 18 on Jay’s YouTube channel

Music Therapy is an original YouTube series developed and produced by viral comedian and musician Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford of Austin-based creative agency Hello Party, financed by Live Nation Studios. In each episode, Jay plays musical therapist to a celebrity guest, blending unscripted conversation and improv with live songwriting before the pair close with an original song they create together. The result lands somewhere between a talk show, a comedy special and a live concert. The first season features Kam Patterson, Ron Funches, Mara Wilson, Brennan Lee Mulligan, Yung Gravy, Matt Friend, Abbey Romeo, Mark Smalls, Tony Jefferson, ASHBY, Josh Johnson and Mandal Mann. Music Therapy was created by Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford (Hello Party) and is directed by Stafford. Brooke Schley serves as showrunner and co-writes the series with Jay. Executive producers are Graham Sicalowski, Robin Rapino, Stella Bulochnikov, Brooke Schley and Matt Sadeghian.

Emma Chamberlain | What Are You Waiting For? | New series premieres early 2027 on Chamberlain’s channel

Emma Chamberlain doesn’t like waiting in line – and wants to understand more about people who do. In this new ongoing series, what starts as an investigation of New York City’s most frequented lines unspools into a thoughtful and expansive meditation on subcultures, fandoms, and what makes our modern world tick. At once whimsical, profound and provocative, and underpinned by Emma’s singular POV, What Are You Waiting For? is a hilarious cultural commentary that not only asks what people are waiting for – but why. The series is executive produced by two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner Joe Lewis, with Amplify Pictures (Fleabag, 100 Foot Wave) serving as the co-studio and production company.

Grace Reiter | Twilight (but better) | New parody film premieres Feb. 18 on Reiter’s channel

Comedian, writer, and actor Grace Reiter (Saturday Night Live) is expanding her comedic universe with Twilight (but better), her second unscripted parody film. #7530. GTA VI is smashing Twitch’s records—and it wants to make sure advertisers don’t miss out

Grand Theft Auto fans across the world are still eagerly anticipating Rockstar’s long-awaited sequel to roll out in their regions. But according to data from Streams Charts, GTA VI has already smashed multiple streaming platform records—including becoming “the most popular gaming category in Twitch history by peak viewers.”

As of publication time, GTA VI has attracted a peak of 3.29 million concurrent viewers on Twitch, 3.19M on YouTube, and 1.5M on Kick.Those totals put it “ahead of every previous game launch tracked by Streams Charts,” the data company said in its report.

Twitch isn’t taking all that buzz—or the dollar signs that come with it—for granted. But GTA also doesn’t exactly fit into the platform’s careful approach to brand safety. So, it’s introducing new tech to ensure that advertisers can cash in on the hype surrounding GTA VI without putting their brand reputations at risk.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Back in September, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told hosts of The Snarketing Podcast that the platform had begun using AI to evaluate whether streamers are squeaky-clean enough for brands to run ads against their content.

“[W]e transcribe streams to figure out ‘Is this appropriate for this brand?’” he said. “So that’s something that we’ve had to invest a lot in to make sure that for a brand, their content is appearing next to creators and content that fits what they’re trying to do.”

That update didn’t come out of nowhere: Twitch has long asked streamers to label their content in certain circumstances where mature themes or imagery are involved.

As Gizmodo noted, this means creators have historically missed out on ad revenue when streaming mature-rated games, “because while streamers can receive donations from viewers, big-time monetization ultimately depends on advertising, and advertisers are generally skittish around things that might frighten the poor sensitive product-buying public.”

Last week, however, Clancy told Bloomberg‘s Romaine Bostick that “one of the challenges in this space is advertisers want to be part of the GTA 6 launch”—they just don’t want their ads to appear alongside the spicier parts of the game.

To solve that problem, Twitch’s new technology will allow brands to run ads on GTA VI streams while also ensuring that (as Clancy phrased it) “any of the parts of GTA 6 that they might not want to have their ads associated with, their ads won’t be associated with that.”

The ins and outs of how that system will actually work remain to be seen. But if it does prove effective for GTA VI, we’ll be watching to see whether Twitch expands the tech to other streams and genres previously dismissed as unsafe for brands.

#7528. Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

The first question marketers ask about every new advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?

It happened with social. It happened with retail media. And now it’s happening with OpenAI.

The debate around ChatGPT advertising has quickly become a comparison with Google Search. Can it deliver lower CPAs? Does it convert as well? Is it ready to compete for performance budgets?

They’re all understandable questions. But they’re the wrong ones.

It’s a mistake to assume conversational AI should behave like search in the first place. The customer journey is fundamentally different. If marketers continue evaluating ChatGPT using search-era metrics, there’s a real risk they’ll dismiss one of the most significant new advertising channels before they’ve understood how it creates value.

Google built the world’s most successful advertising business by harvesting intent.

If a user searches for “cheap hotels in Hawaii,” Google shares a list of relevant results. The commercial intent is already there. The advertiser’s job is simply to be the most relevant answer when the purchase decision is made. But conversational AI works differently.

Instead of typing in a few keywords, a user might go into detail and explain that they’re travelling to Hawaii for a friend’s wedding, that they’re on a tight budget but want their own room, oh, and they’d like to surf while they’re there. That’s no longer a search query; it’s a conversation. And that difference matters.

Rather than simply capturing existing demand, conversational AI helps users explore options and refine priorities before they buy. When the traveler eventually visits the website to book, they’ve often already used AI to compare all the alternatives and understand exactly what they’re looking for.

The advertising opportunity is participating in how intent develops.

One of the first things marketers notice when they begin testing conversational AI is that the acquisition metrics can look uncomfortable.

CPAs can appear higher than those achieved through search. For anyone used to judging performance through traditional attribution, that’s an easy reason to conclude the channel isn’t competitive.

If it looks like search and behaves like search, surely it should produce similar economics. But once you step back and look at the customer journey rather than the click, that conclusion becomes much harder to support.

A user spending several minutes discussing products, asking follow-up questions and refining their requirements is behaving very differently from someone typing a short keyword into Google. They’re effectively qualifying themselves before they ever reach an advertiser’s website.

That means acquisition might cost more, but the customer arriving at the other end can also be significantly better informed and a much stronger commercial fit.

Judging conversational AI purely on CPA risks confusing efficiency with effectiveness.

The measurement frameworks we’ve inherited aren’t suited for where the consumer journey is going.

For more than two decades, performance marketing has been built around clicks because clicks were observable. Attribution models rewarded whichever interaction happened closest to the conversion, giving marketers a practical way to optimize campaigns at scale.

That made perfect sense in an internet dominated by search engines, display advertising and relatively linear customer journeys.

Conversational AI changes that, because the interaction influencing a purchase often happens long before a click ever occurs. And when the eventual conversion happens later through another channel, traditional attribution naturally gives the credit elsewhere.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the initial conversation had little value; it simply means the measurement framework wasn’t designed to capture it.

Early evidence suggests that when marketers move beyond attribution and begin measuring incremental business outcomes instead, conversational AI looks very different from the picture painted by last-click metrics.

AI advertising can work very effectively. But unless marketers are measuring it in a way that reflects how the channel actually influences buying decisions, it can create a colossal education gap.

The conversation today largely centers on whether OpenAI can compete with Google.

A far better question is whether conversational AI should be evaluated like search at all.

Every evolution in advertising has forced marketers to rethink measurement. Social wasn’t simply another display channel. Retail media wasn’t just paid search inside a retailer’s website. CTV couldn’t be judged solely through linear TV metrics.

Conversational AI deserves the same mindset shift.

Google monetized search intent. Conversational AI has the potential to monetize the conversation that creates it.

Those are fundamentally different commercial models. If marketers continue measuring one using the rules of the other, they risk underestimating not only the performance of OpenAI ads, but the role conversational AI is likely to play in the future of digital advertising.

#7527. Another Disney creator deal: YouTube illusionist Zach King joins the Mouse House

Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.

For their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute. Disney says the agreement “will also bring [King’s] signature illusions to new content for Disney+ and [King’s] own channels inspired by Disney’s Hexed, Star Wars, and other Disney films and experiences.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A New Hope. King uploaded the film to YouTube in August, and soon will cross-post it to Disney’s streaming service.

But there’s still more: King will pop up on Disney’s social accounts as well, hosting behind-the-scenes content about the VFX and filmmaking techniques he uses in his content.

“I fell in love with filmmaking and storytelling as a young kid, grabbing my parents’ home video camera and teaching myself to edit,” King wrote in an Instagram post. “A lot of my early homemade films were inspired by the Disney movies and the behind-the-scenes footage they would show in the DVD featurettes. There was always a sense of magic I would see on the screen, and so I’m thrilled to be working with Disney to continue that magic of filmmaking for the next generation of storytellers.”

King has worked with Disney regularly in recent months: He was at its glitzy Created in L.A. event in September, and earlier this month played a game of viral format Cake or Fake? with Hexed (and Arcane, and Sinners, and Spider-Verse, and Hawkeye) star Hailee Steinfeld. But this is his first official, expansive content deal.

“Zach makes the impossible look real, bringing the kind of imagination and originality that has always defined Disney,” Asad Ayaz, The Walt Disney Company’s CMO and Brand Officer, said in a statement. “He brings both a filmmaker’s ingenuity and a fan’s passion to our stories, along with a unique connection with audiences. We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney. That’s what makes this next chapter of our work together so full of possibility.”

As we mentioned above, everyone–including YouTube–has had their eye on Netflix’s obvious poaching efforts…leaving room for Disney to sneak in the back.

In the last couple months, Disney has announced deals with major creators Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect, and Like Nastya. Crucially, these are all development deals–the exact kind of agreement that has YouTube on guard with Netflix.

And Disney’s not quite showing its full hand just yet. During its earnings call Nov. 17, executives only mentioned YouTubers once, in passing and in reference to Disney+’s growing crop of approved creator content.

We suspect more is in the pipeline–and that YouTube may have to start paying creators to turn down Disney deals, too.

#7524. Meet OpenX’s New CEO, An Optimistic Realist

Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.

In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its new CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.

Horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX. In January, the company lost John “JG” Gentry, its CEO for nearly 15 years, after a long battle with cancer.

A 30-year veteran of agencies, advertising and ad tech, Horler previously ran Dentsu Aegis Network in the US and Northern Europe, was COO of Quantcast and, most recently, led creator agency Whalar as chief exec before it was acquired by Accenture earlier this year. He’s still on the Whalar board.

But, given the state of the industry, how was Horler feeling roughly a week in at OpenX? Not too bad. He’s a glass-half-full kinda guy, but he’s also a pragmatist.

“Everybody’s being disrupted,” Horler said. “You can pull the blanket over your head and say, ‘No thanks,’ or you can see an amazing amount of opportunity for companies that are agile and ambitious. I fancy our chances.”

Horler spoke with AdExchanger about Apple’s latest move, whether the sell side has the upper hand right now and the big boots he has to fill.

AdExchanger: Let’s start with the state of play. The assumption for a long time was that as the line blurred between the buy side and sell side, DSPs would come out on top. Now it feels like the sell side has the power. Is that how you see it?

ROBERT HORLER: I’d agree, but it’s complicated. The pendulum has swung toward supply because advertisers want to get closer to the data and the publisher.

For the first time in about 30 years, the bigger agencies are pursuing divergent strategies for how they work with SSPs and DSPs. They all want more control, more orchestration and more influence over the revenue they drive, and I’d hypothesize that SSPs are well placed to deliver that.

Also, no slight to The Trade Desk, but if the biggest cat in the jungle is having this many existential challenges, that tells you something’s going on.

Speaking of big cats, OpenX is suing Google, as is Magnite, PubMatic and Index Exchange. I know there’s not much you can say about OpenX’s lawsuit, if anything, but as an industry observer, what did you think of the fact that Google didn’t have to divest AdX in the federal ad tech antitrust case?

You know, it’s a shame. It’s tough for everybody who thought there would be one, but I can’t say that I’m surprised there wasn’t.

A lot of sell-side players are going buyer-direct. So is everything just everything now? Are the distinctions between buy-side and the sell-side tech no longer meaningful?

For the people who aren’t in it, who don’t work in ad tech or programmatic advertising – and that includes some clients – the lines have always felt quite blurred. That’s not new.

There’s probably not as much difference now as there was, though. Things are converging and overlapping and people are encroaching a bit into each other’s territories as they figure out the brave new agentic landscape. And, of course, there are also pressures that exist within their own businesses.

But what will always be true is that publishers want to generate as much yield as possible and advertisers want to pay as little as possible, as long as it’s still effective, of course. So, yes, perhaps those lines are blurring a bit, but this natural tension will always exist.

I know you’re still settling in, but how about you approaching Apple’s move to block identity vendors in iOS 27?

That’s all I can say right now other than that no one here is walking around and behaving like it’s an extinction event or something.

You spent the better part of a decade on the buy side, including as the US CEO of Dentsu. What do buyers get wrong about the sell side?

I’d flip it, actually. The sell side needs to be simpler to partner with and more able to adapt, and sometimes they forget that. The sell side also underestimates how overwhelmed buyers are with choices.

If you show up with an overly complex sell or a raft of products that you can’t explain in simple language, you’ll just sound like everyone else. Also, don’t underestimate the importance of humanity. Trust is built around people, not just technology.

I wanted to ask about John. He was such a lovely man, and his death was such a loss. How will you keep his legacy alive?

I never got to meet him, and I really wish I had. He was clearly beloved. When I came in for my board interview, I read the remembrance book here and it was really moving. It made me think, “If I get this job, those are big boots to fill.”

The best way to honor him is to continue the mission and build a valuable company where people enjoy coming into work. John clearly believed culture is preeminent and that it’s the people who make a great company, and I want to lead with that in mind.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.
